title: Facade and Flyweight
idea: Facade gives a busy subsystem one simple entry point. Flyweight shares one object for state that repeats, so thousands of uses cost little memory.
points: A facade exposes one method that calls several subsystem classes in order.
Callers depend on the facade, so subsystem changes stay behind it.
Flyweight splits state: shared intrinsic data and per-use extrinsic data.
A factory hands out the shared object, creating each kind only once.

edges.label: placeOrder
edges.caption: The route makes one call. It does not know which classes sit behind the facade.
The facade reserves stock first, because charging for missing stock is wrong.
Then it charges the payment. The order of steps lives in one place.
Finally it creates a shipping label. Swap `Shipping` and the route never changes.

code.title: Facade: checkout
code.caption: Three subsystems behind one method. Add a `Receipts` class and call it in `placeOrder`; line 14 stays the same.

code.title: Flyweight: map pins
code.caption: Four pins share two `Icon` objects. Add more `cafe` pins and watch the icon count.

walk.text: `Icon` holds the heavy, shared part, frozen so no user can change it.
Position is extrinsic: passed into `draw`, never stored.
The factory creates an icon per kind once, then reuses it.
Each pin is a small tuple: kind plus coordinates.
Draw every pin, then compare pins with icons actually created.

pitfalls: Keep a facade thin; business rules in it turn it into a god class.
Do not block direct subsystem access when an advanced caller needs it.
Never mutate a flyweight's shared state; every user of it would change.

quiz.why: The second `get('x')` finds the key and returns the same object, so both names point to one entry.

takeaway: Facade simplifies access; Flyweight shares repeated state to save memory.
